analysis.title: Split Fed left rates unchanged, waiting for more information
key_insights: The Fed left the policy rate unchanged at 3.75-4.00% by a 10-2 vote. Cook and Hammack dissented in favour of a 25 bp hike.

The statement said 'the accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal.' This matches signals from Williams, Jefferson and Waller that there was no urgency to tighten again.
The hold is consistent with the September median projection, which showed one more hike by year-end rather than hikes at both the October and December meetings.
Hammack, Logan and Kashkari dissented in July. Cook is now a fourth member voting for a hike. September minutes showed some members saw hikes as necessary, while many viewed them as insurance.
The statement upgraded economic activity from expanding at a 'solid' pace to a 'strong' pace. Warsh said the economy had strengthened, and he noted that investment is broadening beyond high-tech.

The statement changed 'timelier' to 'timely' return of inflation to target. Warsh cited tighter financial and credit conditions since September and said he was encouraged by progress, including inflation compensation in swaps and inflation expectations moving the right way despite energy prices.

Warsh said he is 'unwilling and unable to call financial conditions tight', which SEB reads as the Fed having more work to do. He still said inflation is too high and pointed to energy and IT-related goods prices.
SEB judges Warsh's language to be more dovish than at Jackson Hole or after the September meeting. SEB reads it as consistent with a December hike but not necessarily a series of hikes.
Warsh described an 'information rich' period ahead, covering geopolitical developments, energy prices and technology changes.

There were no balance sheet changes in the statement. Warsh said the Fed will await the task force recommendations and feed them into first-quarter deliberations next year. Any move to resume shrinking the balance sheet therefore waits until 2027.
From fall 2027, one of eight FOMC meetings will be devoted to strategy, with no rate decision or statement. In 2028, two of eight meetings will be strategy meetings and six will be policy meetings.

Markets first reacted hawkishly to the statement, then read Warsh's comments as dovish. The 2-year yield fell almost 10 bp at the most and the 5-year fell 5 bp from pre-announcement levels. The Nasdaq turned higher and the curve steepened.
Markets price 21 bp for a December hike, almost two full hikes by March, and more than 2.5 but fewer than 3 hikes by end-2027.
SEB forecasts one more hike in December, then no change, then a return to cuts by late 2027.

risk_factors: Upside risks: the ongoing Middle East conflict and persistently high energy prices spreading into other prices.
Downside risks: rising real yields and new bouts of market unrest.
Warsh warned that relative price rises in energy and IT-related goods could broaden across the economy.
vol_and_positioning: Yields rose a couple of bp after the statement and then fell. The 2-year yield was down almost 10 bp at the most and the 5-year was down 5 bp. Longer-dated yields were little changed, so the curve steepened again.
geopolitical: Warsh listed geopolitical developments as a driver of the Fed's next step, and SEB cites the ongoing conflict in the Middle East as an upside risk to inflation.
Cook has come under attack from the White House again. An earlier attempt to remove her was stopped by the Supreme Court.

tension_points.bull_case: Cook and Hammack voted for a 25 bp hike, and some members saw hikes as necessary given their inflation outlook. Warsh said inflation is too high and that financial conditions are not tight.
tension_points.bear_case: Williams, Jefferson and Waller saw no urgency, and many members viewed hikes as insurance. Warsh's language was softer, and he said tighter financial conditions and moves in inflation compensation represent progress.
tension_points.what_invalidates: SEB sees upside risks from the Middle East conflict and energy prices spreading into other prices, and downside risks from rising real yields and new bouts of market unrest.
